name: Akrah
title: Unidentified figure – possible name variant of Akar/Achan
summary: The name Akrah cannot be securely identified as a person in the canonical biblical texts. It does not appear directly as a personal name in the Hebrew Bible or in the New Testament. The most likely connection is to Achar (עכר), also called Achan (עכן), son of Karmi from the tribe of Judah. According to Joshua 7, Achar took some of the devoted things after the conquest of Jericho, which brought defeat upon Israel at Ai and led to severe judgment against him and his household. The similarity between Akrah and Achar may be due to paleographic confusion or dialectal variations in Hebrew manuscript traditions – especially since the letters nun (נ) and resh (ר) are easily confused. Another possible association is the place name Akra, the Seleucid fortress in Jerusalem from the second century BC, but this is a place name with no connection to a biblical person. The Hebrew root ע-ק-ר carries meanings such as 'to uproot' and 'barren', without pointing to any specific biblical figure. Thus, Akrah remains an uncertain entity without clear biblical grounding.

footnotes.text: The name 'Akrah' does not appear as a personal name in the canonical Hebrew or Greek Bible texts. The closest parallel is 'Akar' (עכר), also known as 'Achan' (עכן) in some textual traditions, son of Karmi from the tribe of Judah, mentioned in Josh 7 and 1 Chron 2:7. The variation between the name forms Achan and Akar reflects a textual-critical issue where the letters nun (נ) and resh (ר) can easily be confused in Hebrew manuscripts.

'Akra' (Greek: Ἄκρα) was a fortified garrison in Jerusalem, built by Antiochus IV Epiphanes around 168 BCE during the Hellenistic occupation. The fortress is mentioned in 1 Maccabees and was a symbol of Seleucid control over the city. However, this is a place name, not a personal name.

The Hebrew root ע-ק-ר (ʿ-q-r) has meanings such as 'to uproot' and 'barren'. This root is used in several places in the Hebrew Bible, including regarding barrenness (Gen 11:30; Judg 13:2), but it does not form a basis for identifying a specific biblical person named Akrah.

In the Talmud (Sanhedrin 44a–44b), the sin and judgment of Achan/Akar are discussed in detail. The rabbis discuss the extent of his transgression and the principle of collective responsibility. Some rabbis derive from the name form Akar (עכר) that he 'confused' or 'brought misfortune upon' Israel, a wordplay based on the verb עכר.

Paleographic confusion between similar Hebrew letters is a well-known phenomenon in textual criticism. Especially the letter pairs dalet/resh (ד/ר), nun/resh (נ/ר) and he/het (ה/ח) are prone to copyist errors in manuscripts. Such a confusion could explain how the name form 'Akrah' possibly arose from 'Akar' or 'Achan'.
